# What SB 1383 Means for Your Business


***September 3, 2026***


[California’s Senate Bill 1383](https://calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/) has quietly become one of the most consequential environmental laws in the country. It targets short-lived climate pollutants by dramatically cutting the organic waste sent to landfills—and it places new obligations directly on the businesses that generate that waste. If your operation touches food production, distribution, hospitality or retail in an affected region, this law already shapes how you handle organic material.


The stakes are real.[Organic waste in landfills](https://editions.mydigitalpublication.com/publication/?i=826218&p=18&view=issueViewer) releases methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide. SB 1383 sets ambitious targets: a 75% reduction in organic waste disposal and the recovery of surplus edible food for people in need. For businesses, that translates into concrete compliance requirements, potential penalties and a pressing need for a smarter waste strategy.


Below, we break down what the law asks of you, why regional operators feel the pressure most acutely, and how a proactive program turns a compliance burden into a competitive advantage.


## **Why Food and Agriculture Feel It First**


Few sectors generate organic waste at the scale of food and agriculture. Consider a regional operation like a food manufacturing facility. Producers of that size manage enormous volumes of organic byproduct daily, from processing remnants to surplus product. Under SB 1383, that material can no longer simply head to the landfill.


Affected businesses must now:


- **Arrange organic waste recycling.** Food scraps, green waste and other organics require dedicated collection and diversion.
- **Recover surplus edible food.** Certain generators must donate a portion of edible food to food recovery organizations.
- **Maintain compliant records.** Documentation proves your program meets jurisdictional requirements—and protects you during inspections.
- **Coordinate across multiple sites.** Multi-location operators face a patchwork of local enforcement, each with its own nuances.


Miss these obligations, and the consequences extend beyond fines. Non-compliance risks operational disruption and reputational damage in communities that increasingly value environmental responsibility.


## **Compliance is a Moving Target**


Here’s the challenge many operators discover: SB 1383 is not a one-time checkbox. Enforcement continues to expand, requirements evolve and each jurisdiction interprets the rules differently. Managing that complexity across a regional or national footprint quickly overwhelms internal teams already stretched thin.


That is precisely where a coordinated partner changes the equation. Rather than juggling separate haulers, shifting regulations and inconsistent reporting, you gain a single, unified strategy built around the law’s demands and your operational reality.

## **Bring Your Team Into the Effort**


Compliance succeeds when your people embrace it. A well-designed program pairs naturally with employee environmental initiatives that turn regulatory requirements into shared purpose.


When staff understand why organic waste separation matters—and see the measurable impact of their participation—engagement rises and contamination falls. Simple steps make a difference:


- Train teams on proper sorting at the source.
- Celebrate diversion milestones to reinforce momentum.
- Invite employee ideas for reducing waste before it starts.


These initiatives strengthen compliance, boost morale and signal a genuine commitment to sustainability that customers and communities notice.

They build resilient, efficient programs that recover value, engage their teams and position their brands as responsible leaders.
